title: The Lookup Journey
about: Follow a website name from your device to the server that knows it.

cards.title: The resolver's trip
cards.body:
If the answer isn't in your **cache**, your device asks a **resolver**: a [[server]] that hunts for answers for you. It asks from general to specific:

1. A **root server** points to the `.com` servers.
2. A **[[TLD]] server** points to example.com's server.
3. That **authoritative server** holds the real answer.

cards.prompt: You opened `example.com` a minute ago and need its [[IP address]] again. Where's the **fastest** place to find it?

options.text: In your device's memory of recent answers
By asking the server that runs example.com
options.nudge: That server could be across the world: is anywhere closer that saw this answer a minute ago?

options.text: By searching one big list of every name online
options.nudge: No single list of every name exists: where did a minute-old answer go?

options.text: In your home router's list of where to send packets
options.nudge: Routers work with addresses, not names: what did your own device do a minute ago?

cards.explanation: Your device keeps recent answers in a short-term memory called a **cache**, so a minute-old address is probably still there. No question needs to leave your device.
cards.hint: You asked this exact question a minute ago: where might the answer still be?

cards.prompt: Nobody has looked up example.com lately. Put the lookup steps in order.

items.label: Your device checks its own cache
Resolver asks a root server about .com
Resolver asks a .com server where to go
Answer comes back; caches keep copies

cards.explanation: Your device checks its **cache** first. Then the resolver goes general to specific: **root**, **TLD**, then the **authoritative** server, which holds the real address; copies are saved for next time.
cards.hint: Start with the check that never leaves your device, then go from general to specific.
cards.nudge: Your device checks its own memory before asking anyone; after that, think country, then town, then street.

cards.prompt: Match each [[DNS]] server to its job.

pairs.right: Asks for you and caches the answers
Knows where to find each TLD's servers
Knows who's in charge of each domain

cards.explanation: The **resolver** works for you; **root** points to TLD servers, **TLD** servers point to each domain's authoritative server, and that holds the real answer. Caches only keep *copies*.
cards.hint: Only one server holds the real records; the others ask for you or point the way.
cards.nudge: One works for you, one points to TLDs, one points to domains, and one holds the answer.

cards.prompt:
Every [[DNS]] answer has a **TTL** (time to live): how many **seconds** it may stay in a [[cache]] before it's looked up again.

How many **minutes** is a TTL of **3,600**?
cards.explanation: 3,600 seconds ÷ 60 = **60 minutes**, one hour; then the answer is looked up fresh. 3,600 is the number of seconds, not minutes.
cards.hint: The TTL is in seconds: how many seconds make a minute?
cards.nudge: The question asks for minutes, not seconds: convert first.

cards.prompt: `dig` is another [[DNS]] tool. Run `dig example.com` and find the **TTL**: the number just after the name.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal, with dig's output shortened to just the answer. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Look up example.com and show the answer

success.question: What is the TTL of this answer, in seconds?

cards.explanation: The line reads: the name, the **TTL** (1,800 seconds, or 30 minutes), `IN A` (an internet address answer), then the [[IP address]]. The dot in `example.com.` is how dig writes a full name.
cards.hint: Under `;; ANSWER SECTION:`, look at the number right after the name.
cards.nudge: Don't type the address: the TTL comes straight after `example.com.`, before `IN`.

cards.prompt:
At **11:50** you look up a site (TTL **3,600**). At **12:00** it moves to a new [[IP address]].

When can you be sure you'll use the new one?

options.nudge: Nothing tells your cache the site moved: it keeps the old answer until the TTL runs out.
The TTL started at your lookup, not when the site moved.

options.text: Never: the old address is cached forever
options.nudge: Cached answers can't stay forever: the TTL says how long they may be kept.

cards.explanation: The old answer may stay 3,600 seconds (one hour) from your lookup: **11:50 + 1 hour = 12:50**. In practice some apps and [[resolvers|resolver]] cache a little differently, so owners often lower the TTL before a move.
cards.hint: The TTL clock starts at your lookup: how long is 3,600 seconds?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Your device checks its **cache**, then asks a **resolver**.
- The resolver asks root, TLD, then the **authoritative** server.
- Answers stay cached for their **TTL**, counted in seconds.
